n: In this topic we will examine the action of physical factors on the body. We begin with heat exchange. Normal body temperature is 36-37 °C. At a temperature below 22-25 °C or above 43-44 °C, changes incompatible with life occur in the tissues. Excess heat is removed from the body by radiation 55 %, by sweat 27 %, by conduction 15 % and by excretions 3 %. General action leads to heat stroke or freezing. Local action is manifested as a burn or frostbite.

Heat stroke develops when much heat is produced and little is given off. Conditions for this: high temperature and humidity, absence of wind, a hot workshop and heavy physical work. Clothing that does not let air and moisture through creates predisposition. In cardiovascular diseases, hyperfunction of the thyroid gland, obesity and old age, heat stroke develops more often. Children under one year are very sensitive because thermoregulation is not yet fully formed. That is, the risk depends not only on external conditions but also on the state of the body.

Now the course of heat stroke. In the acute form, consciousness is suddenly lost, coma occurs, and death follows within a short time from cardiovascular and respiratory disturbance. The course may also be gradual: first the central nervous system is depressed and consciousness clouded, then a period of excitation comes, after which weakness, that is, the pre-agonal period, begins. Remember: if the temperature exceeds 42-43 °C, breathing stops as the primary event.

t: Sunstroke and the picture on the body
n: Sunstroke arises when a person stays for a long time in the sun without head covering. Signs: headache, clouding of consciousness and convulsions. A marked rise in body temperature is not characteristic of it. Turning to the picture on the body, in death from heat stroke and sunstroke the cadaveric changes are similar and nonspecific. They are plethora, oedema of the brain and its membranes, and small haemorrhages. Rigor mortis develops quickly and strongly, while cadaveric lividity appears late and scanty.

A thermal burn arises when the temperature in the skin and underlying tissues exceeds 45-50 °C. Its features depend on the type of source, the temperature and the duration. Causes: flame, hot viscous substances, that is, tar, napalm, bitumen, and also water above 60 °C, hot steam, gases and a heated object. There is one more important point here: in areas where the skin is thin, the burn is deeper.

We will consider the degrees of burn in sequence. First degree proceeds with erythema, swelling and pain and passes without trace in 3-4 days. In second degree, blisters with serous fluid appear and heal without a scar in 10-20 days. Third degree is characterised by necrosis. In IIIA the necrosis is in the epidermis and the superficial layer of the dermis, in IIIB it is complete. Here granulation forms in 2-3 weeks, and then a scar remains. Fourth degree involves deep tissues and is characteristic of the action of flame.

t: Determining the source of high temperature
n: The expert determines the source of high temperature from the appearance of the burn. In a burn from hot liquid, hair and clothing are not damaged, and the burn is superficial, in the form of runs. Areas covered by clothing can also be burned. In a burn from flame, hair and clothing are damaged, the wounds are tongue-shaped and deep, and there are traces of soot. "Tongues of flame" are directed upwards. A heated object leaves a deep, limited burn whose shape corresponds to the contact surface. A burn of the airways, however, is characteristic only of steam and hot gas.

To determine the area of the burn, the "palm rule" is used: the surface of the palm makes up about 1 % of the body surface. There are also special tables for determining the area more exactly. The diagram gives the rule of nines. Head and neck 9 %, arm 9 %, front surface 18 %, back surface 18 %, thigh, and also lower leg and foot, 9 %, and perineum 1 %. So, by adding the percentages by body part, the burn area can be assessed.

t: Life-threatening burns and writing the diagnosis
n: The limits of life-threatening burns are as follows. A burn of more than 10 % of the body surface in III-IV degree, more than 15 % in III degree or more than 20 % in II degree is considered an injury dangerous to life. A burn of the airways, that is, oedema and narrowing of the glottis, is also dangerous to life. In the diagnosis the burn is written as a fraction: the area in the numerator, the degree in the denominator. For example, 10 % / II or 30% (10%) / II-III.

Burn disease develops if a first-degree burn occupies more than 50 % of the body surface, and second- to fourth-degree burns more than 10-15 %. Four periods are distinguished in its course: shock, which may last up to 2-3 days, then intoxication, 1-2 weeks, then the period of complications and recovery. If it is combined with a burn of the airways and the toxic action of the products of combustion, that is, carbon monoxide, the probability of death increases two times or more.

t: Vitality of the action of flame
n: Now the vitality of the action of flame, that is, the question whether the flame acted while the person was alive. In a fire, death most often results from carbon monoxide poisoning, and after death the body is charred by the flame. Soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach is a sign that the flame acted during life. Carboxyhaemoglobin in post-mortem flame action does not exceed 20 %, while in vital action it reaches 60 %. Blood is taken from the heart chambers and deep vessels.

There are other signs of vitality too. When the skin of the eyelid is spread, the alternation of damaged and undamaged areas, that is, the "crow's feet" sign, indicates vital action. A burn of the airways, abundant clotted blood, arterial thromboses and fat embolism of the pulmonary vessels are also signs of vital flame action. One more sign is in the fluid of the blisters: in vital burn blisters the protein content is twice as high as in those formed after death.

t: Burnt body: epidural haematoma and posture
n: In a burnt body, the epidural haematoma and the posture are taken into account. A traumatic epidural haematoma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura mater. One formed after the flame is crescent-shaped and not attached. In flame, moisture evaporates and the muscles become denser and shorten, so the "pugilistic posture" forms, and the skin may also split. The body of an infant turns to ashes in 2-3 hours, that of an adult in about 20 hours.

Now the general action of low temperature. The action of cold is intensified by high humidity, wind, clothing unsuited to the season, fatigue, hunger and intoxication. Children and the elderly are sensitive. In cold water death may come in 1-1.5 hours. On sudden immersion in cold water, death occurs from vascular collapse or cold shock even before deep hypothermia. When body temperature falls to 30-28 °C, cortical function is disturbed. At the final stage, at +25...+22 °C, death often results from primary cessation of breathing.

External signs of freezing. The first is the "posture of a frozen person": the arms are drawn to the chest, the legs to the abdomen. In heavy intoxication it may be absent. Exposed areas are bluish and slightly swollen. Around the mouth and nose there are icicles, and on the eyebrows and eyelashes hoarfrost; these are Raisky's signs. "Goose skin" is also observed. In men the testis is contracted and the scrotum drawn up to the inguinal canal, which is Puparev's sign. The skin and cadaveric lividity are pinkish-reddish in tone.

We move to the internal signs of freezing. The internal organs are plethoric, the stomach empty and small, which is Pukhnarevich's sign. There are small haemorrhages in the renal pelves, which is Fabrikantov's sign. Vishnevsky's spots are small haemorrhages in the mucosa of the stomach and duodenum. They occur in 80-90 % of cases and are found even after 6-9 months. However, when death occurs quickly, Vishnevsky's spots may be very scanty or absent, especially in children.

t: Microscopy and freezing of the body
n: In microscopy, microcirculatory spasm, oedema and small haemorrhages are seen. Proliferation of the epithelium of the straight tubules of the kidney is regarded as Kasyanov's sign. In heavy intoxication the alcohol in blood may be low and in urine high. In a frozen body the volume of the brain increases, the skull bones may fracture and the sutures separate. Therefore the body is thawed at room temperature or in warm air or water up to +50 °C.

Local frostbite is most often seen on the fingers and toes, ears, nose and cheeks. Degrees: in first degree a reddish-bluish tone, 3-7 days. In second degree blisters, 10-20 days. In third degree necrosis, 1-2 months. In fourth degree necrosis down to the bone. Purulent processes may develop as complications: phlegmon, osteomyelitis and sepsis.

Although electrical injury makes up 1-2.5 % of all injuries, it holds one of the leading places for disability and death. In most cases it is an accident from technical electric current. Suicide or homicide is rare, and lightning very rare. A feature of electric current is that it cannot be detected without a special instrument. Injury occurs at the site of contact and along the path of the current, and the energy is converted into other forms.

t: Properties of electric current: type, voltage, strength
n: Properties of electric current: type, voltage and strength. Up to 500 V alternating current is more dangerous than direct. At 500 V they are equal; above that direct current is more dangerous. The international norm of safe voltage is 24 V, while most deaths are observed at 220-380 V. At voltage above 3000 V, because of the electric arc, local burn and death are less common. A current of 50 mA causes cardiovascular and respiratory failure, and 100 mA leads to death in most cases. A frequency of 40-60 Hz is extremely dangerous, and above 10 000 Hz does not injure.

t: The body and conditions of action
n: The action of current also depends on the body and the conditions. Children, the elderly and pregnant women are more sensitive. Cardiovascular diseases, hypoxia, intoxication, trauma and heat stroke lower the resistance. The increase in resistance differs by blood, mucosa, liver, kidney, muscle, brain, lung, ligament, cartilage, nerve, bone and skin; morphological change occurs in the region of bone and skin. Moist skin and sweating create favourable conditions for the current, so death is more frequent in summer. With a prolonged current of more than 25 mA, spasm of the respiratory muscles occurs, and from 80 mA fibrillation.

Current loop and step voltage. Single-pole connection of a body insulated from the ground usually does not endanger life. However, at high voltage injury is possible also through an electric arc. It is dangerous if the current passes through the heart and brain: the upper, left, left oblique and left full "current loops". Step voltage is the potential difference across a step of 0.8 m around a broken conductor. For safety, one must not approach closer than 10 m.

In the general action of electric current, ventricular fibrillation of the heart, disturbance of breathing, that is, electrogenic asphyxia, electrogenic shock and injury of small vessels are observed. In chemical action, coagulative necrosis forms on the anode side and colliquative necrosis on the cathode side, and impregnation of the skin with metal particles occurs. Thermal action is manifested by burns and by "pearl beads" on the bone, with a diameter of 1-5 mm. Mechanical action leads to joint dislocations and bone fractures.

The electric mark forms at the points of entry and exit of the current. The local temperature reaches 120 °C, and the mark is clearly visible on the palm and heel. Its appearance is round or oval, firm, with raised edges and a depressed centre, that is, crater-shaped. The surrounding skin is unchanged and the hair is not singed. The colour of metallisation depends on the conductor: bluish-green for copper, yellow-black for iron, grey for aluminium. Remember: on thin or moist skin, in 10-20 % of cases there is no mark.

t: Electric burn and kinds of death
n: An electric burn forms at high voltage. The local temperature is above 120 °C, all layers of the skin undergo necrosis, the burn is painless, and there is no inflammation around it. In survivors the size of the injury becomes clear after 2-3 weeks and turns out to be several times greater than the initial one. According to Avdeev, the kinds of death are: ultra-rapid, slow, interrupted and late. In apparent death, that is, vita minima, resuscitation is recommended until cadaveric lividity appears.

On atmospheric electricity, that is, lightning. In lightning the voltage is millions of volts and the current hundreds of thousands of amperes. The injuring factors: electric current, light, sound and the blast wave. Tearing of the skin, singeing of hair and melting of metal parts of clothing are observed; changes similar to the electric mark also occur. The "lightning figure" is a tree-like red-pink pattern and is specific. It disappears within several hours or days, so it is photographed at once.

Barotrauma arises from a sharp change in atmospheric or water pressure. It occurs in diving, flight, explosion, high mountains and a pressure chamber. Mechanical action includes decompression sickness, "boiling" of fluids, barotrauma of the lungs, ears and nasal sinuses, and compression of the body. Biological action results from a change in the partial pressure of gases: oxygen or CO2 poisoning, hypoxia and the narcotic action of nitrogen.

How does pulmonary barotrauma arise? At a depth of 10 m the hydrostatic pressure is 2 times, and at 20 m 3 times, the atmospheric. When scuba equipment is used, pulmonary barotrauma is observed in 80 % of cases and drowning in 20 %. If breath is held during ascent from under water, the pressure in the lungs rises sharply by 80-100 mm Hg, and the bronchi and alveoli rupture. Air passes through the pulmonary veins to the heart, and arterial air embolism, especially in the cerebral arteries, leads to death. Bilateral pneumothorax is also possible.

We will consider gas poisoning. The neurotoxic form of oxygen develops at a pressure above 2.5-3.0 MPa: loss of consciousness and convulsions occur. The pulmonary form appears at 1.0-1.5 MPa on exposure longer than 2 hours. CO2 poisoning arises when CO2 in the breathing air is 3 % or more. Nitrogen dissolves 5 times better in fat than in blood and causes a state similar to alcoholic intoxication. In rapid ascent, dissolved nitrogen forms gas bubbles; this is decompression, that is, caisson, disease. In the body, gas-containing blood clots are found in the right chambers of the heart and in the veins.

Low pressure and altitude sickness. In the unacclimatised, altitude sickness begins at 3500-4000 m. At 5000-7000 m uncompensated hypoxia is added, and at 6000-8000 m decompression disorders. When the pressure falls to 6 kPa, that is, 45 mm Hg, which is at 18000 m, tissue fluids "boil" and subcutaneous emphysema forms. In a body found in a mountainous area, death may also be from other causes, so inspection of the scene with a specialist is important.

We turn to the action of radiation. Radiation injuries are caused by alpha and beta particles, neutrons, gamma rays and X-rays. Neutrons, gamma rays and X-rays have high penetrating ability. Cell division dies down, especially in bone marrow, skin, intestine and gonads. Forms by dose: up to 10 Gy the bone marrow form, 10-20 Gy the intestinal form, 20-80 Gy the toxaemic form, above 80 the cerebral form.

t: Radiation sickness and forensic medical tasks
n: Acute radiation sickness consists of three stages: primary reaction, up to 3-4 days; latent period, 2-4 weeks; and the period of marked clinical signs. Death often results from infectious complications. In the body, numerous haemorrhages in the skin, tissues and internal organs are found, with destructive changes in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Tasks of the examination: determining the type of injuring factor, the properties of the source, the dose, the number and time of exposures, and the severity of the bodily injury.

t: Examination of living persons: when ordered
n: Now the examination of living persons. These are the examinations most frequently carried out in practice, and they are ordered in criminal, civil and administrative cases. The following are established: the character and severity of bodily injury; sexual conditions and crimes; state of health, simulation, dissimulation, aggravation and artificial disease; and also age. Examinations are carried out in the outpatient department and departments of forensic medical expert institutions, and in some cases in medical institutions.

t: Bodily injuries: questions and legal classification
n: Questions resolved in bodily injuries: the type, location and properties of injuries; the type of weapon; the mechanism of formation; the age of injury; the degree of severity. The Criminal Code distinguishes grave, moderately severe and minor bodily injuries. Severity is determined by the forensic medical rules. A moderately severe injury means impairment of health for more than 21 days or permanent loss of working capacity of 10-33 %; this is Article 105 of the Criminal Code.

Criteria of degree of severity: danger to life, duration of impairment of health, permanent loss of working capacity, loss of function of an organ, mental disorder, termination of pregnancy and disfigurement. See the table. The main sign of a grave injury is danger to life, loss of ≥33 % or loss of an organ. In a moderately severe injury, >21 days or 10-33 %. A minor injury, short-term, is defined by >6 and ≤21 days or ≤10 %.

t: Procedure for conducting the examination: general algorithm
n: In conducting the examination, the following laws are relied on: the Criminal Code, Code of Criminal Procedure, Civil Code, Code of Civil Procedure, Code of Administrative Liability, the laws "On the Protection of Citizens' Health" and "On Forensic Examination", and the instruction. The procedure and methodology are determined by the features of the event and the tasks set. General algorithm: understanding the circumstances of the event, examining the originals of medical documents, enquiry about the circumstances of the injury, studying the injury on inspection, additional examination if necessary and, at the end, documenting the conclusion.

The originals of medical documents are submitted. The person who ordered the examination is responsible for their reliability. The person's identity is confirmed by a passport, military ID or birth certificate. In sexual conditions and crimes, two photographs are also needed. In the enquiry it is established when, where, by whom, with what, on what area of the body and how many times the action was applied. The enquiry ends with complaints.

On inspection, the type, location, shape, size and colour of the injury, contamination and the state of the surrounding skin are studied. Photography is carried out only with the person's permission. When a person of the other sex is undressed, the investigator leaves. Minors are inspected in the presence of a parent or teacher, and those lacking capacity in the presence of a legal representative. Inspection of a person under treatment is carried out only if health allows, in the presence of an employee of the institution, and is recorded in the case history. The clinician advises.
